Forest Specification for Multi-Forest Models

forest.Rd

One forest of a model of several forests. Such a model fits the mean as a sum of forests, each multiplied by columns of the data: y ~ forest(x1 + x2) + forest(x1 + x2, basis = dose) is \(a_1 f_1(x) + a_2 \cdot \mathrm{dose} \cdot f_2(x)\), where each \(f\) is a forest and each \(a\) a coefficient the sampler draws. A forest is written as a term of a bart or dbarts formula, as in that example, or as an element of the forests list of dbarts or dbartsSpec: forests = list(forest(), forest(basis = dose)). Either way vars is the predictors the forest splits on and basis is what it is multiplied by. Every setting is per forest and stated on the forest.

The constructor is not exported: it resolves by bare name inside the arguments that take it, and elsewhere is written dbartsForests$forest(...); see dbartsForests.

Usage

forest(
    vars = NULL, basis = NULL, sd = NULL,
    n.trees = NULL, base = NULL, power = NULL, amplitude = NULL,
    interactions = NULL, blocks = NULL,
    proposal.probs = NULL, n.perturb.cuts = NULL, treeShift = NULL)

Arguments

vars

The predictors this forest splits on. In short:

  • It is the one argument given without its name: forest(x1 + x2). Every other argument is given by name.

  • Left out, the forest splits on every predictor of the fit.

  • In a formula it is terms joined by +, as on the right of any model formula: forest(x1 + x2), forest(log(x1) + factor(g)), forest(. - z).

  • In a forests list the same terms select among the fit's predictors, forest(x1 + x3), forest(. - x2); names or positions do too, forest(c("x1", "x3")), forest(c(1, 3)).

  • A one-sided formula is its right-hand side, the tilde accepted and never required: forest(~ x1 + x2), or a formula held in a variable, f <- ~ x1 + x2 and then forest(f). A formula with a left-hand side is refused.

  • A name of a predictor is that predictor. Anything else is read where forest() is called, at that moment.

The rest of this item is the detail of each.

In a formula given to bart or dbarts it is written as the right-hand side of a model formula of the forest's own: forest(x1 + x2), forest(log(x1) + factor(g)), forest(. - z), where . is every column of data but the response and - removes a term. The fit's predictors are the terms of all of its forests, each once, and a forest splits on the columns of its own terms; a term that gives several columns, such as poly(x1, 2) or a factor under factors = "indicators", is all of them. Predictors may also be named, as forest(c("x1", "x2")): a name of a column of data is the term that name written out is, and any other name is a column of the predictors as the fit builds them, one of a factor's indicator columns for instance. A position is not taken in a formula. An offset() and an intercept term (1, 0 or - 1) belong to the fit and are written beside the forests, not inside one. A removal written beside the forests takes its term from the forest with no basis and from no forest that names predictors of its own: the forest with no basis has the terms of the formula with its forest() replaced by what is inside it and every forest with a basis left out. So y ~ forest(.) - x3 + forest(x3, basis = z) and y ~ . - x3 + forest(x3, basis = z) are one model, in which the second forest alone splits on x3; a removal that leaves the first forest no predictor is refused. Written with no first argument, that forest is every predictor the other forests name, less what is removed beside it. A removal of a term the forest with no basis does not have is passed by, as R passes it by in a plain formula: y ~ x1 + x2 + forest(x3, basis = z) - x3 is the model without the removal. update cannot take a term out of a forest(): update(f, . ~ . - x3) returns f unchanged when x3 stands inside one.

In a forests list it selects among the fit's predictors, in one of two ways. When a name in it is a predictor of the fit, it is read as terms in the same way: forest(x1 + x3), forest(. - x2), forest(. - log(x1)). There . is every column of the fit's predictors, and a term names a predictor as the fit holds it, by its term label when the fit has a formula and by its column name when it has a matrix, written as code or as a backticked name; a term that names no predictor is refused, a removed one too. Anything else is a value: it is evaluated once, where forest() is called and at that moment, and gives the predictors' names or their positions among the fit's columns: forest(c("x1", "x3")), forest(c(1, 3)), or a variable holding either. A warning that evaluation raises is kept and raised when a fit uses the value. A name or a position given twice is refused, and so are a logical, a factor and a formula: the multiplier of a forest is its basis, by name. A column with no name is selected by position or by . only, and a name that two columns share is refused. A number is a position only as the whole argument: among terms, as in forest(. - 2), it is refused, and a column named 2 is written backticked. With a factor expanded to indicator columns, removing one of them, as forest(. - g.u), leaves the forest able to separate that level through the others; remove the factor, forest(. - g), to keep it out.

A name of a predictor is that predictor, and anything else is read where forest() is called, at that moment. A forest built in a loop, by lapply(names, forest, basis = z) or by Map() therefore keeps the selection each call was given, whatever its variables hold by the time the model is fitted, and a forest saved to a file carries its selection with it. A variable that does not exist yet when forest() is called is not looked for later. One case needs care: a predictor hides a variable of yours with the same name, so in forest(x1) with a predictor x1 and a variable x1 that holds names, the predictor is meant. Where the two could meet, hand the value over: do.call(forest, list(vars = nms)).

Any forest may be restricted, a single declared forest included: given the same residual scale estimate, that fit is the fit on the named columns alone, and its other columns report no splits. The estimate is taken from every column unless sigest states it, so the two fits agree draw for draw when it does. On a single forest split.probs = dart() beside vars lays its Dirichlet over the named columns, every other column reporting probability 0, and split.probs keeps its ratios among the named columns and must give one of them a positive probability (see dbartsPriors). On every forest of a hazard fit the period column the fit appends is always allowed, named or not: vars restricts the columns the caller supplied. The restriction holds for the sampler's life; $setModel refuses a model that states another, or none.

basis

What the forest is multiplied by. In short:

  • A name of a column of data is that column: basis = dose.

  • A basis is one numeric column, or a factor, a character column or a logical column of two levels, with a coefficient for each level. A number is one column, whatever its values: basis = z for a z of 0s and 1s is one coefficient, and basis = factor(z) is the two levels.

  • I(dose + age) is one column, their sum. Several columns, dose + age, and three or more levels are refused: give each column, or each level but the first, a forest of its own.

  • Anything that is not a column of data is read where forest() is called, at that moment, with or without a tilde written in place: forest(basis = w), forest(basis = ~ w).

  • A formula held in a variable, b <- ~ w and then forest(basis = b), is read the same way, when forest() is called, and is left as you made it.

  • cbind() is refused: write its one column alone, or give each column a forest of its own.

The rest of this item is the detail of each.

What it does. With a basis of columns \(B_1, \ldots, B_K\) the forest \(f\) enters the fit as \((\sum_k a_k B_k(x_i)) f(x_i)\), each column with a coefficient \(a_k\) of its own, called its amplitude: \(K = 1\) for a numeric column, and the two columns of a factor's levels, \(K = 2\). A forest with no basis is multiplied by a single coefficient. A model has one forest with no basis, or none; every other forest states one, and a model whose only forest has a basis is refused.

Writing it. A basis is the right-hand side of a model formula, without the tilde, and means what it means in lm:

  • a name is a column: basis = dose;

  • + separates columns: dose + age is two columns, which this version refuses (below);

  • arithmetic is written inside I(): I(dose + age) is one column, the sum, and I(dose / 30) is dose rescaled;

  • a function of columns is a term, as in lm: log(dose), scale(age) and poly(dose, 1);

  • a factor, a character column or a logical column of two levels gives one column for each, none left out: factor(z) for a z of 0 and 1 is the two columns whose coefficients are \((b_0, b_1)\), in the order of the levels;

  • dose:age is one column, the product;

  • there is no constant column unless 1 asks for one, and 1 + dose, a column of ones beside dose, is refused, while 0 + dose and dose - 1 are dose.

A basis is either one factor (or character or logical column) or numeric columns; the two are not mixed in one forest. The forest does not center or scale a basis, so a multiplier that should be standardized is written so: basis = scale(age). A numeric column constant over the observations in the likelihood has no standard deviation to take the default sd from, and is refused unless sd is stated.

One size. In this version a basis is one numeric column, or a factor, a character or a logical vector of two levels, counted on the rows the fit keeps once a level they leave empty is dropped. Three or more levels are refused, with the form to write, a forest for each level but the first: forest(x1, basis = arm == "b") + forest(x1, basis = arm == "c"). Several numeric columns are refused however they are written, dose + age, poly(dose, 2), splines::ns(dose, 3), a matrix, or a factor's indicator columns handed over as numbers, with the form to write, a forest for each column: forest(x1, basis = dose) + forest(x1, basis = age); indicator columns are handed over as the factor itself. 1 + dose is refused for its constant column: write basis = dose. Each is refused drawn or held, at every place a basis is given, and a basis handed over as a value is told the form in words.

Which kind it is. The class of the basis decides whether the forest multiplies levels or numbers, the same way at every place a basis is given: forest() written as code or with a value, dbartsData's bases, $setForestBasis and predict's bases. A factor, ordered or not, a character vector and a logical vector are levels, with a coefficient for each: in the order of a factor's levels, in sorted order for a character vector, FALSE then TRUE for a logical vector. An integer or a double is numbers, whatever its values, and a numeric matrix is its columns. The values are never looked at to decide: a column of 0s and 1s is one column with one coefficient, and is two levels only when written factor(z) or as a logical vector. A matrix of characters or of logicals, and a factor matrix, is refused, one of a single column included, since a vector is levels and a matrix is numbers: hand over its column as a vector, cm[, 1]. An array of one dimension is its vector. A data frame and any other class are refused too. Handed over as a value, the refusal names the class; written as code, a class a model frame does not take, a data frame or a list, is refused in R's own words.

The kind is fixed when the forest is created. A forest created with no basis cannot be given one, and a forest of levels keeps the same levels, in the same order, for as long as the sampler lives, so that coefficient \(j\) multiplies level \(j\)'s rows after any replacement. See $setForestBasis in dbartsSampler and the bases argument of predict in bartBT for what a replacement takes.

A level that no row the fit keeps has gives no column and no message, written as code or handed over as a value: factor(z, levels = 0:2) of a z with no 2, or a factor of three levels under a subset that leaves two of them, is the two columns of the levels that remain. The count is made after the rows are cut, and fewer than two levels left is refused. A row of weight zero is a row the fit keeps.

A missing value is looked for on the rows the fit keeps, after subset and the na.action, as lm looks for one in its variables. On a kept row it is refused. On a row the fit drops it is not looked at, so a basis fits the same way written as code or handed over as a value. NA is not a level: a factor made with addNA() or exclude = NULL that has a kept row at NA is refused, and the remedy is to give that level a name, as in levels(f)[is.na(levels(f))] <- "none". With no kept row at it the NA level is dropped like any other level no row has.

Some forms a model formula would take are refused, each by name and with what to write instead: * between terms (write I(dose * age) for the product, or give dose, age and I(dose * age) a forest each for all three); a term multiplied or divided by a number (write I(dose / 30)); - between terms, other than - 1; ^, /, %in% and | between terms; .; an offset(); cbind() (write its one column alone, or give each column a forest of its own); and a term that calls one of normal, fixed, student, cauchy, linear, gp, cgm, dart, chisq, chi, invchi, forest or varianceForest, since a prior is not stated on a term of a basis.

Names of the columns. They are named as coef(lm(y ~ 0 + <basis>)) names them: dose; factor(z)0, factor(z)1; and, for a basis of several columns, which is read and named before it is refused and whose refusal quotes the names, dose, age, poly(dose, 2)1, poly(dose, 2)2 and (Intercept) for the column of ones. They are the column names of data@bases[[f]] on the sampler. A forest's label, where its place in a forests list has no name, is the text of its basis, "scale(age)", or forest<i> for a forest with no basis or with one given as a value; see dbarts. Wherever a method or an extract or predict takes a forest, a string is a forest's label (failing an exact match, the label that is the same code, so "I(dose / 30)" finds I(dose/30)), a number is its position as base R reads a list element by number, and forest<i> names position i, though a per-forest margin of a fit is named by the forests' labels. A string is never a position: "2" is a forest labeled "2" or none. A string that is one forest's label and another position's name, or the same code as two labels, is refused.

Rows. A basis has a value for every row of data, and is cut to the rows the fit keeps: data and subset are each evaluated once, for the fit, and the basis is given the same rows in the same order, less those the na.action drops. So with data = d[sample(nrow(d)), ] or subset = sample(n, 100) the basis has the rows the fit has. scale(), poly() and anything else a term computes across rows, I(age - mean(age)) among it, are computed on every row of data, as in lm, whatever subset keeps. A level of a factor that no kept row has gives no column. Refused are a missing value in a row the fit keeps, where lm would drop the row; a factor, a character column or a logical column with one level on the rows kept; and a numeric column that is zero on all of them.

New rows. predict builds the basis again from the new rows, as predict does for lm. Taken from the fitted rows are the center, scale and knots of scale(), poly(), ns() and bs(), and the levels of a factor. Everything else is computed again on the rows given: I(age - mean(age)) uses the mean of the new rows, and factor(dose > median(dose)) their median; see SafePrediction. Every column of data the basis names must be among the new rows, a factor's columns keep the order of the fit's levels, and a level the fit did not have is refused. A basis given as a value cannot be built again: give it at the new rows through predict's bases argument.

Where a name is found. It depends on who wrote the code.

In a call of forest() that you write, as in a forests list or for a forest built ahead of the fit, a name of a column of data is that column. Every other variable of yours that the code uses is copied when forest() is called. This is so whether or not a tilde is written in place: forest(basis = ~ I(dose + age)) is forest(basis = I(dose + age)). A forest built in a loop therefore keeps what each call was given,


    fs <- list(forest())
    for (k in c(10, 30))
      fs[[length(fs) + 1]] <- forest(x1, basis = I(dose / k))

is one forest multiplied by dose / 10 and one by dose / 30, at the fit and at predict, whatever k holds later, and a saved forest carries its numbers with it. A variable that does not exist when forest() is called is not looked for later, and is refused. What R or an attached package supplies, a function such as scale or a constant such as pi, is not copied: a basis that names a column of data looks it up when the model is fitted. With no data frame, as with the matrix interface and dbartsSpec, there is no column to name and every variable is yours.

One case needs care: a column of data hides a variable of yours with the same name, whether that variable holds a column, a set of names or a one-sided formula. Where the two could meet, hand the value over: do.call(forest, list(basis = w)) for a column you hold, list(basis = as.name(nm)) for a column of data by its name, list(basis = f) for a one-sided formula, and list(vars = nms) for predictors by name.

A formula made elsewhere, held in a variable or handed over as above, is read in the same way and at the same moment, when forest() is called: a name of a column of data is that column, and every other variable the formula uses is copied, as it is then, from where the formula was made. What counts is when forest() is called, not when the formula was made. In


    fs <- list(forest())
    for (k in c(10, 30)) {
      f <- ~ I(dose / k)
      fs[[length(fs) + 1]] <- forest(x1, basis = f)
    }

each forest has its own k, because forest() is called inside the loop. Formulas made in a loop and given to forest() only after it all see the last k: a formula holds its environment and no value, as everywhere in R. A variable changed after forest() is called changes neither the fit nor a prediction. The formula itself is not touched: it is the formula you made, in its environment, and nothing is assigned there.

A forest() term inside the formula of bart or dbarts is part of that formula and is read with it, as R reads a formula, with a tilde or without: in data and then where the formula was written, when the model is fitted and again by predict. Change a number such a term uses between the fit and the prediction and the prediction changes, with no message.

An argument that lapply(), Map() or another function of base R writes for you, as in lapply(columns, forest, vars = "x1"), is a value handed over, whatever the data's columns are called. A name or a call that such a function is handed and passes on, as in Map(forest, nms, MoreArgs = list(basis = quote(dose))), is code, as it is through do.call().

A value. What is handed over as an object, through do.call() or in a call built by a program, is used as it is: a numeric vector or matrix is its columns, and a factor, a character vector or a logical vector is its levels, as written as code. Its column keeps the name it has. Its forest's label is forest<i>. It has one row for every row of data and is cut to the rows the fit keeps; a value already cut to those rows is refused by name. A level that no row the fit keeps has gives no column, whether data, subset or the na.action is what empties it. A value that the rows kept leave with one level, or one numeric column that is zero on all of them, is refused as the same basis written as code is. A single string or number is refused: basis = "dose" names no column, so write basis = dose.

A basis is stated here or on the data object, not both: dbarts given an already-built dbartsData refuses this argument, the data object's own bases being where it is stated then, while dbartsSpec takes a data object and installs the bases declared here in place of those it carried. After creation a basis is replaced by $setForestBasis, whose formula is read at once, where it was made; see dbartsSampler.

A lone forest carrying a basis is refused, the coefficients being what distinguish a forest from another. For varying coefficients declare an intercept forest plus one basis forest per covariate, forests = list(forest(), forest(basis = z1), forest(basis = z2)), or use one forest with linear() leaves.

n.trees, base, power

This forest's tree count and tree-structure prior. Each one stated here governs this forest, and each one left out takes the default of the forest's kind, whatever the forest's place. A forest with a basis has 50 trees at base = 0.25, power = 3 - shallower and fewer than a prognostic forest's, the modulating surface normally being the smoother of the two. The forest with no basis has the fitting function's: bart's n.trees or the control's, and its power and base. The fitting function and the forest with no basis state one setting between them: bart refuses its own n.trees, power or base beside one stated here, the default's own value included, the two being the same setting, and a control that names n.trees beside one stated here is the same count. Where every forest has a basis the fitting function's tree count and tree prior have no forest to belong to, and one that is stated is refused, the default's own value included: state it on a forest. A sampler's control@n.trees and model@tree.prior hold its first forest's.

sd

The size of what this forest contributes, in the response's units: the units of \(y\) for a continuous response, and of the latent index under "probit" and "logistic", where the link's own error has standard deviation 1 and \(\pi/\sqrt{3}\). One number; a name on it is ignored. What it is the size of depends on what multiplies the forest.

No basis. The forest enters as \(a\,f(x)\), and sd is the size of \(a\,f(x)\).

A factor (a factor, a character vector or a logical vector, of two levels). The forest enters with one coefficient for each level, and sd is the size of the difference between the two: the treatment effect where the levels are control and treated.

A number \(w\). A column that is an ordinary covariate should be centered: basis = scale(w), or basis = I(w - c) for a reference value \(c\). The other forests describe the response where \(w\) is 0, and a column that never comes near 0, an age or a year, makes them an extrapolation and the fit poor, with nothing in the chain to show it. A dose or an exposure, where 0 means none, is left as it is. The forest enters as \(w\,(a\,f(x))\), and sd is the size of \(a\,f(x)\), the change in the response for one unit of \(w\); the term at an observation has size \(|w|\) sd. The column is used as given: it is never centered and never divided, so a stated sd is per unit of \(w\), and the same sd with \(w\) in grams and in milligrams states two priors a thousand times apart.

Where the coefficient is held (amplitude = fixed()) it is 1, what it multiplies is the basis, and "size" is the prior standard deviation, exactly. Where it is drawn the size is itself uncertain, and sd is its prior median.

Not stated, sd for a forest with no basis is twice \(\mathrm{sd}(y)\) under a continuous response where its coefficient is drawn, the size bart gives its forest (a quarter of the response's range) where it is held, and one unit of the link's error under "probit" and "logistic" either way; \(\mathrm{sd}(y)\), or that unit, for a factor; and for a number that same size for one standard deviation of the column, \(\mathrm{sd}(y) / \mathrm{sd}(w)\) per unit, held or drawn. None of these depends on how many forests the model has. A default fit is then the same fit whatever units \(w\) is in. \(\mathrm{sd}(y)\) and \(\mathrm{sd}(w)\) are taken once, over the observations in the likelihood when the sampler is created (those subset and the missing-value handling keep, with a positive weight, and not masked out), and kept: replacing the column, the weights or the mask later does not move the prior, unless the column is replaced with $setForestBasis(updateBasisScale = TRUE), and a copy, a saved and reloaded sampler and a sampler made again from its own control, model and data keep it. Where those observations hold fewer than two distinct values of the response, both are taken over every observation, under one warning (two by the route of dbartsSpec and new(), see its active). "probit" and "logistic" read no \(\mathrm{sd}(y)\), and where fewer than two observations are in, \(\mathrm{sd}(w)\) is taken over every one, under one warning; two or more that hold one value of \(w\) are refused. \(\mathrm{sd}(y)\) is of the response net of its offset; on a gaussian response that does not vary over those observations it is a quarter of the window of width one the response is then scaled by. \(\mathrm{sd}(w)\) is kept with the data, in its basis.scale slot (see dbartsData), and $getLeafPrior(f)$basis.scale reports it. A caller who replaces a column during burn-in and wants the default of the new one replaces it with $setForestBasis(f, w.new, updateBasisScale = TRUE), which takes \(\mathrm{sd}(w)\) again over the observations in the likelihood then (see dbartsSampler). A column that is constant over those observations has no standard deviation and needs sd stated.

A treatment belongs in a factor or a logical vector, where sd is the treatment effect. Written as a 0/1 number it is scaled as any number: \(\mathrm{sd}(z)\) is 0.5, 0.4 and 0.22 at 50, 20 and 5 percent treated, so the default effect is 2, 2.5 and 4.6 times the one factor(z) gets; sd = sd(y) on the number states the factor's. The same holds for a coding written as a number and held, basis = z - 0.5 with amplitude = fixed().

A held coefficient cannot adapt to an sd that is too small. At the default it is sized for a slope of about one \(\mathrm{sd}(y)\) per \(\mathrm{sd}(w)\); where the effect may be larger, under "probit" and "logistic" above all, state sd or let the coefficient be drawn.

A default is not a stated number: $getLeafPrior(f)$sd reports the number of the response's units it comes to, a numeric forest's named by its column, and $getLeafPrior(f)$sd.stated is FALSE. A stated number is kept as written and divided by the unit once, at each creation. A control or a forests list taken to other data states the same numbers in that data's units, and the sampler made from it derives its own. It is one number, positive and finite. A vector of any other length and anything that is not a number are refused. The one forest of a model of one forest takes it as the fitting function's leaf.prior = normal(sd = ), in the same units, and stating the size at both places is refused.

It is the one argument a live sampler restates: $setLeafPrior(forests = list(forest(sd = ), ...)) states it from then on, also where it is the number in force, and leaves the recorded \(\mathrm{sd}(w)\). $getLeafPrior(f)$leaf.prior returns the statement, forest(sd = ) where one was stated and forest() where none was, and forest() written back leaves its forest as it is (see dbartsSampler). A forest's kind is fixed at creation: $setForestBasis refuses to give a basis to a forest created without one, and moves no forest's prior.

print of a fit and show of a sampler give a short block of one line for each forest of a model of several: its label, what it multiplies, for a numeric column the mean and sd it has over the observations in the likelihood as they stand, and the sd the forest resolved to. For a numeric column that is its sd per sd of the column as it now stands, named by the forest's label, the size of the forest's term over one sd of the column in the response's units: for a default it is \(\mathrm{sd}(y)\) (the link's error sd under "probit" and "logistic") wherever the column, and the observations it is read over, are those the default was taken from, and for a stated sd it is that sd times the column's sd. Where the column is constant it is the sd per unit. For a factor it is the sd between the two levels. The sd per unit of a numeric column, which is what forest(sd = ) states, is in the full block and in the reader. The last line of the short block says where each forest's prior is to be had in full: summary() of a fit, which prints the full block, or $getLeafPrior() of a sampler, which returns it. The summary of a fit and the creation of a sampler with verbose = TRUE give the full block. Its header gives the unit the sds are in: \(\mathrm{sd}(y)\), as taken above, or the link's error sd. A numeric line gives the sd per unit and per sd of the column and adds the column's range; every line adds whether the sd was stated or is the default, and whether the coefficient is held. A default whose column has another sd over the observations now in the likelihood than the one it was taken from (the column replaced, the weights or the active rows changed, or, under "gaussian", every observation read because those in the likelihood held fewer than two values of the response) says so. A fit made with keepFits = FALSE keeps no bases or labels and gives no block. Two things to look for. The mean of a numeric column, in either block, and its range, in the full one: a mean far from 0 is a column that never comes near 0, an age or a year, and should be centered, unless 0 means none, as for a dose; and one wild value shows in the range, and moves the mean and sd. And the figure per sd of the column, in either block, the size of the forest's term over one sd of the column (sd times the column's sd): for a default it is \(\mathrm{sd}(y)\) on every numeric line whose column, and the observations it is read over, are those the default was taken from, so a line that differs has had its column or its observations changed, and for a stated sd it is where a number in the wrong units shows. Nothing in the fit warns of either.

interactions, blocks

Optional interactions and blocks constraints on this forest. The arguments of the same names on dbarts are those of the forest with no basis, wherever it stands, so one stated there and on that forest is refused as one constraint given twice. A forest with a basis states its own here, and where every forest has one those arguments of the fitting function are refused. Holding the two forests to different structures is the calibrated-additivity idiom - an additive or low-order modulating forest beside a free prognostic one. A blocks partition covers the columns the forest may split on, i.e. the vars subset when one is given, and the forest's own tree count.

amplitude

The prior on this forest's coefficient: the one a forest with no basis carries, or one for each level of its basis. Left out, it is drawn each sweep, under a normal prior on a forest with a basis and, on a forest with none, a half-Cauchy prior whose median is the forest's sd. student(df) draws it under a Student-t prior with df degrees of freedom, finite and at least 1; student() is student(1), the half-Cauchy. With a basis the t is scaled so that its median size is the normal's, so the forest's sd keeps its meaning, the prior median of what the forest contributes, and only the tails move: a coefficient ten times its median size has prior probability 0.06 under student(1), 0.005 under student(3) and about \(10^{-11}\) under the normal. That tail lets the coefficient follow a multiplier whose scale is far from what the sd states, at the cost of slower mixing along the ridge the coefficient shares with the forest's leaves. With no basis the coefficient's size is the forest's size, its median the sd or, where none is stated, the size the forest has by default, so student(1) restates that default and Bayesian causal forests' prognostic prior is written amplitude = student(1), sd = 2 * sd(y). The draw is exact, a normal coefficient given a variance drawn from its inverse-gamma conditional. fixed() holds it for the sampler's life, the choice being made at creation, wherever the forest stands: a held coefficient is 1, and what it multiplies is the basis, so a forest with no basis enters at 1, a forest on a numeric column at the column as given, and a forest on a factor, a character or a logical vector of two levels at 0 for the first level and 1 for the second. The forest is then held out of the first level and enters at full size for the second, so it is the second level's difference from the first. Another coding is another basis, and another size is sd, which a held coefficient makes exact: the forest's contribution then has prior standard deviation sd. A held forest with no basis that states no sd has the size bart gives the one forest of an ordinary fit under a continuous response, a quarter of the response's range, and one unit of the link's error under "probit" and "logistic". A numeric column held enters as given, its forest at full size wherever the column is 1: basis = z - 0.5 held is the forest times -0.5 and 0.5. A held coefficient cannot adapt to an sd that is too small; where the effect may be larger, state sd or let the coefficient be drawn. fixed alone is taken as fixed(), and student alone as student(); no other value is, a response family among them. Outside the argument that takes them the constructors are dbartsPriors$fixed() and dbartsPriors$student(). The prior is stated for a forest of a model of several, at creation; a model of one forest has no coefficient to give a prior, and its size is drawn through the fitting function's leaf prior, as leaf.prior = normal(k = chi(1.5, 2)) or normal(sd = invchi(1.5, s)). $getLeafPrior(f)$amplitude reads it back.

proposal.probs, n.perturb.cuts, treeShift

This forest's tree moves - its proposal mixture, perturb window and level-shifting step - as dbartsControl describes each. Each one stated here governs this forest and each one left out takes the control's: $setControl changes a forest's setting only where the forest states none, and one stated here is fixed for the sampler's life. A stated proposal.probs is a whole mixture, filled against the package defaults as dbartsControl()'s is and not edits to the control's, so an omitted birth is 0.5. A forest frozen by its own mixture is still grown by n.grow.sweeps and replaced by warm.start, as under the control's, and treeShift acts on the constant leaves of two or more trees, as the control's does. n = and p = each abbreviate more than one argument, so write n.trees and power in full.

Details

With two forests, the second carrying a two-level factor basis, this is the Bayesian causal forest \(y = a\,\mu(x) + b_z\,\tau(x) + \epsilon\): a prognostic forest \(\mu\) over every predictor, a modulating forest \(\tau\) over the columns vars allows, and the amplitudes \((a, b_0, b_1)\) joining them, read back with $getForestAmplitudes. Gaussian, "probit" and "logistic" responses; under a latent family the combination is the index rather than the mean, on the link's own fixed scale, and "aft", "ordinal" and "nbinom" are refused at creation naming what each is missing.

What the defaults put on the combined location, since under a latent family that location IS the index and no drawn \(\sigma\) stands between it and the fitted probabilities. At two forests of the shipped shape - one carrying no basis - a probit model's prior puts \(P(p < 0.01 \mathrm{~or~} p > 0.99)\) at 0.238, which is the shipped single-forest binary default's own 0.239. A forest's default does not depend on how many forests the model has, so each forest added widens the prior on the combined location. When every forest carries a factor the induced prior standard deviation of the index is \(1.049\sqrt{K}\) latent units, 1.484 at \(K = 2\), which is 0.989 of the classic \(k = 2\) binary leaf-scale budget; a numeric column at its default contributes 1.484 for each standard deviation of the column the row is from 0. When one forest carries none, its amplitude is Cauchy and has no variance to enter that budget with, and the others contribute \(1.049\sqrt{K - 1}\), 0.699 of the budget at \(K = 2\). Where many forests share one index, state their sd. Read the values in force off $getLeafPrior(f)'s sd entry, in the response's units.

Both forests' leaf scales come from the model's own calibration map rather than from the leaf prior, which is why a k hyperprior, a non-default k, a named leaf-prior sd, and a linear or Gaussian-process leaf prior are refused when a second forest is declared, the size of the forest with no basis being written on the forest, as forest(x1 + x2, sd = 2), in the response's units as normal(sd = ) is. In a model of several forests this sd states one forest's share of the combined location's prior, per unit of a numeric basis, where normal(sd = ) states a single forest's whole spread. Every value here is validated at fit time, and anything today's engine cannot honor is refused there by name rather than dropped.

In a bart or dbarts formula each forest() term is one forest of the model, without a separate forests = list: y ~ forest(x1 + x2) + forest(x1 + x2, basis = z). A term stands at the top of the formula's right-hand side, joined to the others by +; a forest() crossed with another term, as z:forest(x1 + x2) or z * forest(x1 + x2), is refused with the forest() to write in its place. The forest with no basis is the forest with no multiplier and the model's first, wherever it is written; a forest's default tree count and tree prior go by whether it has a basis and not by where it is written. It may be left as plain terms, y ~ x1 + x2 + forest(x1 + x2, basis = z), which is the same model, but a formula has one such forest: plain predictor terms beside a forest() with no basis, and two such terms, are refused. Alone, y ~ forest(x1 + x2) is the single-forest fit y ~ x1 + x2, in every family that takes a formula. The other forests keep the order they are written in. forest() may also be written there as dbartsForests$forest(). A term's predictors and its basis are read as code; every other argument is evaluated where the formula was written. The same basis written in a formula's term and in a forests list is the same columns on the same rows, and so the same model.

Value

A dbartsForest specification object, resolved when a sampler is built.

See also

dbartsForests, dbarts, bart, dbartsSpec, interactions, blocks

bart's ‘Formula Terms’ section is the full term grammar - the forests of a formula, a forest's predictors, and the refusal list - of which the ‘Details’ paragraph above is the constructor-side summary.

Examples

set.seed(0)
n <- 100L
x <- matrix(runif(n * 3), n, 3, dimnames = list(NULL, c("x1", "x2", "x3")))
z <- rbinom(n, 1L, 0.5)
y <- 2 * x[, 1] + z * (1 + 2 * x[, 3]) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.2)

sampler <- dbarts(x, y,
                  forests = list(forest(),
                                 forest(x1 + x3, basis = factor(z),
                                        n.trees = 25L, sd = 1.5)),
                  control = dbartsControl(n.chains = 1L, n.trees = 25L,
                                          n.samples = 20L, n.burn = 20L))
samples <- sampler$run(20L, 20L)
amplitudes <- sampler$getForestAmplitudes()

# the induced prior sd of the combined location, read off the sampler rather
# than recomputed from the call: forest 2 is the one carrying a basis
calibration <- sampler$getLeafPrior(2L)
basis <- sampler$data@bases[[2L]]
# its coefficients' prior variance is 1/2
indexSd <- sqrt(calibration$k.scale^2 * 0.5 * rowSums(basis^2))

# the same model written in a formula, the first forest written out; the
# columns of a basis are named as lm() would name them
d <- data.frame(y = y, x1 = x[, 1], x2 = x[, 2], x3 = x[, 3], z = z,
                w = 50 + 10 * rnorm(n))
written <- dbarts(y ~ forest(x1 + x2 + x3) +
                    forest(x1 + x3, basis = factor(z), n.trees = 25L, sd = 1.5),
                  d, control = dbartsControl(n.chains = 1L, n.trees = 25L))
colnames(written$data@bases[[2L]])
#> [1] "factor(z)0" "factor(z)1"

# a standardized multiplier: predict centers and scales the new rows by the
# training rows' mean and sd of w
fit <- bart(y ~ forest(x1 + x3) +
              forest(x1 + x3, basis = scale(w), n.trees = 10L),
            d, n.trees = 10L, n.samples = 10L, n.burn = 10L,
            n.chains = 1L, n.threads = 1L, keepTrees = TRUE)
#> estimating the starting sigma by a dense linear regression on 100 rows and 2 columns; see 'sigest'
#> family = "auto": continuous response detected, fitting family = "gaussian"; set 'family' to override
#> 
#> Running BART with numeric y
#> 
#> number of trees: 10
#> number of chains: 1, default number of threads 1
#> tree thinning rate: 1

#> 	k prior fixed to 2.000000
#> 	degrees of freedom in sigma prior: 3.000000
#> 	quantile in sigma prior: 0.900000
#> 	scale in sigma prior: 0.008161
#> 	power and base for tree prior: 2.000000 0.950000
#> 	use quantiles for rule cut points: false
#> 	level fiber gibbs step: auto
#> 	proposal probabilities: birth/death 0.60, swap 0.00, change 0.40, perturb 0.00, rule_gibbs 0.00; birth 0.50; perturb window 1
#> data:
#> 	number of training observations: 100
#> 	number of test observations: 0
#> 	number of explanatory variables: 2
#> 	init sigma: 0.948004, curr sigma: 0.948004
#> 
#> Cutoff rules c in x<=c vs x>c
#> Number of cutoffs: (var: number of possible c):
#> (1: 100) (2: 100) 
#> forests, sd in the response's units (sd(y) 1.139):
#>   1 forest1: no basis; sd 2.278 (default)
#>   2 scale(w): numeric basis, mean 0, sd 1, range -2.666 to 1.923; sd 1.139 per unit, 1.139 per sd (default)
#> Running mcmc loop:

#> DONE BART

predict(fit, d[1:3, ])
#>              1        2        3
#>  [1,] 2.927474 1.455927 1.616158
#>  [2,] 2.760547 1.257952 1.637542
#>  [3,] 2.992327 1.244774 1.607548
#>  [4,] 2.534323 1.379762 1.449334
#>  [5,] 2.417520 1.363156 1.109988

#>  [7,] 3.029302 0.936659 1.071813
#>  [8,] 2.460682 1.142985 1.244382
#>  [9,] 3.112798 1.896018 1.416407

# forests built in a loop: each keeps the number its own call was given
forest <- dbartsForests$forest
forests <- list(forest())
for (k in c(25, 100))
  forests[[length(forests) + 1L]] <- forest(x1, basis = I(w / k))
looped <- dbarts(y ~ x1 + x3, d, forests = forests,
                 control = dbartsControl(n.chains = 1L, n.trees = 10L))
vapply(looped$data@bases[-1L], function(basis) basis[1L, 1L], 0) * c(25, 100)
#> [1] 58.93674 58.93674

# two columns are a forest each, with a coefficient each; I() holds arithmetic
perColumn <- dbarts(y ~ forest(x1 + x3) + forest(x1, basis = z) +
                      forest(x1, basis = I(w / 50)),
                    d, control = dbartsControl(n.chains = 1L, n.trees = 10L))
lapply(perColumn$data@bases[-1L], colnames)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "z"
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "I(w/50)"
#>
